sections.title: Basic Concept of Counting Figures
sections.content: In Counting Figures, the task is to find the total number of triangles, squares, rectangles, or other shapes formed within a given figure. In such questions, several lines connect with each other to form many small and large shapes. Therefore, not only small shapes but also larger and combined shapes must be counted.

sections.title: Basic Method for Counting Triangles
sections.content: If several lines combine to form triangles in a figure, first count the smallest triangles. After that, count the larger triangles formed by combining two small triangles. Finally, count the largest triangles formed by the entire figure. This is a 2–3 step process that ensures no triangle is missed.

sections.title: Counting Squares in a Grid
sections.content: If a figure is a 2x2 grid, first count the small 1x1 squares. After that, count the larger 2x2 square. Similarly, in a 3x3 grid, first count 1x1 squares, then 2x2 squares, and finally the 3x3 square.

sections.title: Method for Counting Rectangles
sections.content: While counting rectangles, do not count only squares but also rectangles with different lengths and widths. First count the smaller rectangles, then count the larger rectangles formed by combining two or more blocks.

sections.title: Figures in Squares with Diagonals
sections.content: If diagonals are drawn inside a square, they create several small triangles. In such figures, count the small triangles first, then the larger triangles formed by combining two small triangles, and finally the triangles formed by the entire square.

sections.title: Minimum Number of Straight Lines
sections.content: Sometimes questions ask the minimum number of straight lines required to form a particular figure. To solve such questions, carefully count each outer edge and internal line while avoiding duplicate counting.

sections.title: 2–3 Step Counting Process
sections.content: Step 1: Count the smallest shapes. Step 2: Count the larger shapes formed by combining two or more small shapes. Step 3: Count the largest shape formed by the entire figure.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: Students often count only the smallest shapes and forget the larger ones, count the same shape twice, or miss diagonal shapes while counting only straight ones.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Counting Figures, always count from smallest to largest. First count the basic shapes, then combined shapes, and finally the largest shape formed by the entire figure.

tricks.title: Small to Large Strategy
tricks.explanation: Always start counting from the smallest shapes and gradually move toward larger shapes. This prevents missing any figure.
tricks.example: First count small triangles, then triangles formed by combining two small ones, and finally the large triangle.

tricks.title: Simple Method for Counting Grid Squares
tricks.explanation: In a grid, first count 1x1 squares, then 2x2 squares, then 3x3 squares, and so on.
tricks.example: In a 2x2 grid, there are 4 small squares and 1 large square. Total = 5 squares.

tricks.title: Rectangle Identification Trick
tricks.explanation: Any area formed between two vertical and two horizontal lines is a rectangle.
tricks.example: In a 3x2 grid, both small and large rectangles must be counted.

tricks.title: Triangles Formed by Diagonals
tricks.explanation: If a square has one or two diagonals, first count small triangles and then larger triangles formed by combining them.
tricks.example: When both diagonals are drawn in a square, 8 small triangles are formed.

tricks.title: Line Counting Method
tricks.explanation: While counting lines, observe each straight segment separately and avoid overlapping counts.
tricks.example: If 4 points lie in a straight line, they form 3 line segments.

tricks.title: Symmetrical Shape Trick
tricks.explanation: If the figure is symmetrical, count one part and multiply by the number of identical parts.
tricks.example: If one half of the figure has 6 triangles and the other half is identical, total = 12.

tricks.title: Identifying Overlapping Shapes
tricks.explanation: Sometimes two small shapes combine to form a larger one, so always check for combined figures.
tricks.example: Two small triangles can combine to form one larger triangle.

tricks.title: Count the Whole Figure at the End
tricks.explanation: Often the entire figure itself forms a larger shape that students forget to count.
tricks.example: Among many small squares, the complete large square also counts as one.

tricks.title: Segment Marking Technique
tricks.explanation: Mentally divide the figure into smaller parts to make counting easier.
tricks.example: First count triangles on the left side, then those on the right.

tricks.title: Quick Triangle Identification
tricks.explanation: Whenever three lines form a closed region, it represents a triangle.
tricks.example: If three lines create a closed area, it forms one triangle.
